<reason>Both sides were sharp, well-grounded, and format-compliant, but Side B (PRO) won the decisive exchanges. A's two pressure questions were genuinely dangerous—the coercion contradiction and platform-consent entrenchment—but B answered both directly and well: the decoupling answer (under opt-in, refusal forfeits only ad relevance, not the service) resolved the coercion trap, and the observation that small publishers run contextual ads rather than cross-site dossiers blunted the entrenchment route. A's rejoinders (decoupling is "a hope, not a mechanism"; login standards are giant-owned) were real but more speculative. A's audit answer to B's invisible-harm question was solid, yet B's flip—that CON's fallback is always "real consent is impossible, so never ask"—captured the high ground. B's closing flip of A's loyalty-program evidence was the most original and damaging move of the debate, converting A's best new support into proof that opt-in works when the industry believes in the deal. A's aphoristic style ("burns the harvest and calls the ashes consent") kept it competitive, but B made the debate easier to decide and left more routes alive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's second rebuttal: the decoupling answer (refusing tracking under opt-in costs slightly relevant ads, not the service) plus the point that small publishers never needed behavioral dossiers, which together defused both of A's pressure questions and forced A onto speculative ground for the rest of the debate.</best_rebuttal>
